texts.arguments: 3. Mr. Pravin Gondalia, learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has submitted that though accused has some case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about sentence imposed by the courts below. He has requested to consider the subsequent amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act whereby Sections 51 and 52 have been added and under the said sections, only fine is to be imposed. Therefore, he has requested to maintain conviction but modify the sentence and impose fine only. 4. In support of his above submissions and in support of his above request, Mr. Gondalia, learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner accused has heavily relied upon the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Nemi HC-NIC Page 2 of 6 Created On Mon Oct 02 03:30:46 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/79/2010 JUDGMENT Chand vs. State of Rajasthan dated 17/03/2016 passed in Criminal Appeal No.214 of 2016. 5. Though served, nobody appears on behalf of original complainant-Food Inspector. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and more particularly the fact that charge is only of sub- standardization of goods and request is made by learned advocate appearing for the petitioner and considering the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Nemi Chand (supra), she has requested to pass appropriate order. 6. Shah, learned Additional Public Prosecutor and considering the facts and circumstances of the case more particularly when the charge against the petitioner is only of sub standardization of the goods and that original accused was convicted for the offence punishable under Sections 2(i-a)(a) and Section 7(i) of the Act and was convicted under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Act, considering the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Nemichand and amendment in the Act by Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Sections 51 and 52 have been added and under said Chandubhai Jethabhai Gajera vs State Of Gujarat & on 22 September, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/24138135/ 2 sections only fine is laviable, decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Nemichand (supra) squarely applies. 7. In the case of Nemi Chand, (supra), the Hon'ble HC-NIC Page 3 of 6 Created On Mon Oct 02 03:30:46 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/79/2010 JUDGMENT Supreme Court has considered similar request and has observed as under: "2. It is not in dispute that the charge against the appellant was only of sub-standardization of goods. Mr. Sushil Kumar Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that though the appellant has some prima facie case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence which has been imposed by the courts below. He has, in this behalf, argued that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Section 16A was added and under the said section, only a fine is leviable. He has drawn our attention to the judgment of this Court in "T. Barai V. Henry Ah Hoe and Another" [1983 (1) SCC 177] wherein this Court held that since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court. In the said judgment, the Court held as under :- "22. It is only retroactive criminal legislation that is prohibited under Article 20(1). The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law. This finds support in the following passage from Craies on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 388-89: "Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law. Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for Chandubhai Jethabhai Gajera vs State Of Gujarat & on 22 September, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/24138135/ 3 the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon. They are certainly retrospective, and literally both concerning and after the facts committed. But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law, but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence for the purpose of conviction.... There is a great and apparent difference between making an unlawful act lawful and the making an innocent action criminal and punishing it as a crime."
